subject: Urology
title: BPH & Prostate Carcinoma
subtitle: Prostate anatomy, benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate cancer
sourceNote: Built only from the uploaded BPH 6(1) lecture. The bank preserves the lecture organization and treatment pathways without adding external guideline details or drug names.

cases.title: Classic BPH with Mixed LUTS
cases.scenario: A 67-year-old man presents with frequency, urgency and nocturia together with weak urinary stream, intermittency, straining and a sense of incomplete emptying. DRE shows an enlarged, smooth, rubbery-firm prostate with rectal mucosa sliding over the gland.
cases.ar: رجل 67 سنة عنده irritative وobstructive LUTS، والـDRE يظهر enlarged smooth rubbery-firm prostate مع sliding rectal mucosa.
questions: What is the most likely diagnosis?
Classify his urinary symptoms.
Describe the expected DRE findings in this condition.
List the basic investigations.
Outline treatment according to symptom severity.
answer: Diagnosis: benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
Irritative symptoms: frequency, urgency and nocturia. Obstructive symptoms: weak stream, intermittency, straining and sense of incomplete emptying.
DRE: enlarged prostate, rubbery firm consistency, smooth surface and sliding rectal mucosa over the gland.
Basic investigations: urinalysis to exclude infection, serum creatinine, serum PSA and ultrasonography (abdominal US or TRUS).
Mild symptoms: watchful waiting. Moderate symptoms: medical treatment using alpha-blockers or 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors. Surgery is reserved for the stated indications.
cases.trap: Do not judge symptom severity from prostate size; the lecture states that size does not necessarily determine the severity of LUTS.
cases.memory: BPH = mixed LUTS + smooth rubbery-firm enlarged prostate.

cases.title: BPH Pathology and Progressive Bladder Effects
cases.scenario: An older man has only a slightly enlarged prostate but marked urinary symptoms. Ultrasound later shows increasing post-void residual urine and, in a late stage, bilateral hydronephrosis.
cases.ar: مريض كبير عنده أعراض شديدة رغم أن حجم البروستاتا بسيط، وبعدها ظهر residual urine ثم bilateral hydronephrosis.
questions: From which prostatic zone does BPH commonly arise?
Describe the pathology of BPH.
State the two necessary etiological factors mentioned in the lecture.
Describe the compensated, decompensated and late pathologic effects.
What important relation between prostate size and symptoms is demonstrated?
answer: BPH commonly arises from the transitional zone.

It arises as adenomatous tissue, expands and compresses normal prostatic tissue, forming a false capsule with a line of cleavage. Hyperplastic acini vary in size and are lined by one or more layers of cells.
The etiology is unknown, but aging and a normal testosterone level are necessary factors.

Compensated stage: hypertrophy of bladder muscle. Decompensated stage: bladder dilatation with accumulation of post-void residual urine. Late stage: bilateral hydronephrosis, obstructive uropathy and renal failure.
Prostate size does not necessarily determine symptom severity.
cases.trap: A markedly enlarged prostate may cause only minor LUTS, while a slightly enlarged prostate may produce significant symptoms.
cases.memory: Transition zone adenoma -> false capsule -> bladder compensation then decompensation.

cases.title: Acute Urinary Retention in BPH
cases.scenario: A man with previous LUTS suddenly becomes unable to urinate. He has a painful palpable and percussible bladder.
cases.ar: مريض BPH أصبح فجأة غير قادر على التبول، وعنده painful palpable bladder.
questions: What is the diagnosis?
Differentiate acute from chronic urinary retention as described in the lecture.
List the complications of BPH.
When does urinary retention become an indication for surgical intervention?
answer: Diagnosis: acute urinary retention complicating BPH.

Acute retention: painful palpable/percussible bladder and inability to urinate. Chronic retention: non-painful bladder that remains palpable or percussible after voiding; the patient may be incontinent.
Complications: hematuria, acute or chronic retention, infection and stone formation, hernia and piles due to straining, and renal failure.
Refractory urinary retention is an indication for surgery.
cases.trap: Pain and complete inability to void point to acute retention; chronic retention may be painless and associated with incontinence.
cases.memory: Acute = painful and cannot void; chronic = painless residual bladder after voiding.

cases.title: Chronic Retention with Obstructive Uropathy
cases.scenario: An elderly man has a non-painful distended bladder that remains palpable after he passes urine. He has overflow incontinence, bilateral hydronephrosis and impaired renal function.
cases.ar: مريض عنده painless bladder ما زالت palpable بعد التبول، مع overflow incontinence وhydronephrosis وrenal impairment.
questions: What type of retention is present?
Which pathologic stage of BPH does this represent?
Which basic investigations are particularly relevant?
Which surgical indications are present?
List the available surgical interventions.
answer: This is chronic urinary retention.
It represents bladder decompensation; late disease may produce bilateral hydronephrosis, obstructive uropathy and renal failure.
Relevant basic investigations include serum creatinine and ultrasonography, in addition to urinalysis and PSA.
Hydronephrosis or renal impairment and refractory retention are indications for surgery.
Surgical options: TURP, laser prostatectomy, open prostatectomy, and minimally invasive techniques including PAE, echolaser, prostatic urethral lift and water-vapor treatment (Rezum).
cases.trap: A bladder that remains palpable after voiding is the key lecture feature of chronic retention.

cases.title: Selecting BPH Investigations and Treatment
cases.scenario: Two men have BPH. The first has mild symptoms, while the second has moderate symptoms without hydronephrosis, renal impairment, stones or refractory retention.
cases.ar: مريضان BPH: الأول أعراضه mild، والثاني moderate من غير surgical indications.
questions: List the basic investigations for both patients.
List the additional investigations mentioned in the lecture.
What is the treatment of the first patient?
What is the treatment of the second patient?
Name the two medical drug groups.
answer: Basic investigations: urinalysis, serum creatinine, serum PSA and ultrasonography (abdominal US or TRUS).
Additional investigations: uroflowmetry, cystoscopy and CT.
Mild symptoms: watchful waiting.
Moderate symptoms: medical treatment.
Medical groups: alpha-blockers and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.
cases.trap: Do not list surgery merely because the prostate is enlarged; use the lecture indications.
cases.memory: Mild watch; moderate medicate; operate only for indications.

cases.title: When BPH Requires Surgery
cases.scenario: A patient with BPH has failed medical treatment and has recurrent refractory retention. Imaging also shows a bladder stone.
cases.ar: مريض BPH فشل مع العلاج الدوائي وعنده refractory retention وbladder stone.
questions: Enumerate the indications for surgical intervention in BPH.
List the types of surgical intervention mentioned in the lecture.
Identify the procedure illustrated on lecture page 21.
answer: Indications: failed medical treatment, refractory urinary retention, hydronephrosis or renal impairment, and bladder stone.
Types: TURP, laser prostatectomy, open prostatectomy, and minimally invasive techniques (PAE, echolaser, prostatic urethral lift and water-vapor treatment/Rezum).
The illustrated procedure is transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP).
cases.trap: The lecture does not use prostate size alone as an indication for surgery.
cases.memory: Failure, retention, upper-tract/renal damage, or stone -> surgery.

cases.title: Latent Localized Prostate Cancer
cases.scenario: A 66-year-old asymptomatic man has an abnormal routine DRE and raised PSA. Staging shows disease confined to the prostate.
cases.ar: رجل 66 سنة بدون أعراض، اكتُشفت المشكلة في routine DRE وPSA، والورم ما زال localized داخل البروستاتا.
questions: What clinical form of prostate cancer is this?
How is prostate cancer suspected?
What establishes the definitive diagnosis?
List the staging investigations.
Outline treatment of localized disease.
answer: This is a latent tumor: asymptomatic and discovered during routine DRE or PSA.
Prostate cancer is suspected on the basis of DRE and/or PSA.
Definitive diagnosis depends on TRUS biopsy.
Staging investigations: multiparametric MRI, isotopic bone scan and PSMA PET-CT.
Localized disease: radical prostatectomy; radiotherapy may be an alternative (external beam or brachytherapy).
cases.trap: PSA and DRE raise suspicion; the lecture states that definitive diagnosis depends on TRUS biopsy.
cases.memory: DRE/PSA suspect -> TRUS biopsy confirms -> MRI/bone scan/PSMA stage.

cases.title: Risk Factors and Pathology of Prostate Cancer
cases.scenario: A 58-year-old man of African race has an affected brother and an inherited BRCA2 mutation. DRE suggests a hard prostatic nodule.
cases.ar: رجل 58 سنة، African race، أخوه مصاب وعنده BRCA2، والـDRE يوحي بـhard nodule.
questions: Enumerate the risk factors in the lecture.
Where is the macroscopic lesion commonly found?
State the common microscopic type.
List the less common histologic types.
What is the basis and role of Gleason grading?
answer: Risk factors: age over 50, African race, family history in a father or brother, and inherited gene mutations such as BRCA1 and BRCA2.
Macroscopic picture: hard nodule in the peripheral zone.
Microscopic picture: adenocarcinoma with varying degrees of differentiation.
Less common types: small cell carcinoma, transitional cell carcinoma, neuroendocrine tumors and sarcomas.
Gleason grading depends on glandular pattern differentiation and is a prognostic tool.
cases.trap: BPH commonly arises in the transitional zone; prostatic carcinoma commonly arises in the peripheral zone.
cases.memory: Cancer: peripheral hard nodule, usually adenocarcinoma, graded by glandular pattern.

cases.title: Obstructive Prostate Cancer Mimicking BPH
cases.scenario: An older man presents with LUTS similar to BPH, but DRE and PSA raise suspicion of malignancy.
cases.ar: مريض كبير عنده LUTS شبه BPH، لكن الـDRE وPSA أثاروا الشك في prostate cancer.
questions: What clinical form of prostate cancer is described?
What are the three clinical forms listed in the lecture?
How is the diagnosis confirmed?
Which investigations are used for staging?
answer: This is an obstructive tumor presenting with LUTS like BPH.
Clinical forms: latent, obstructive and occult tumor.
Confirmation: TRUS biopsy.
Staging: multiparametric MRI, isotopic bone scan and PSMA PET-CT.
cases.trap: LUTS do not automatically mean BPH; prostate cancer can present as an obstructive tumor.
cases.memory: Cancer can be latent, obstructive or occult.

cases.title: Occult Prostate Cancer with Bone Metastases
cases.scenario: A man presents with bone pain before any urinary complaint. Imaging demonstrates osteoblastic lesions in the spine, pelvis and ribs.
cases.ar: مريض ظهر بألم عظام قبل أعراض البول، والأشعة فيها osteoblastic lesions في spine وpelvis وribs.
questions: What clinical form is this?
What percentage of cases is stated in the lecture?
Describe the routes of spread.
Describe the characteristic bone metastases.
Which staging investigations are appropriate?
Outline treatment of advanced disease.
answer: This is an occult tumor presenting with symptoms of metastasis.
The lecture states that 5% of cases present this way.
Direct spread to adjacent structures; rectal invasion occurs late because of Denonvilliers fascia. Lymphatic spread is to pelvic lymph nodes. Blood spread is to bone, liver and lung.
Bone metastases preferentially involve the spine, pelvis and ribs and are mostly osteoblastic.
Staging investigations: multiparametric MRI, isotopic bone scan and PSMA PET-CT.
Advanced disease: hormonal therapy/androgen deprivation therapy.
cases.trap: The lecture emphasizes osteoblastic, not osteolytic, bone metastases.
cases.memory: Occult 5% -> metastatic symptoms; bone = spine/pelvis/ribs, mostly osteoblastic.

cases.title: Stage-Based Prostate Cancer Management
cases.scenario: Four patients have: (A) a small tumor entirely within the prostate and not detected by DRE or imaging; (B) a palpable tumor still confined to the prostate; (C) extracapsular spread to seminal vesicles; and (D) spread to pelvic organs, lymph nodes or bone.
cases.ar: أربع حالات تمثل مراحل مختلفة من localized إلى metastatic prostate cancer.
questions: Assign stages I-IV to the four descriptions.
What treatment is listed for localized tumors?
What alternative local treatment is mentioned?
What is used for advanced disease?
When is active surveillance considered?
answer: Stage I: small tumor entirely within the prostate, not felt on DRE or seen on imaging. Stage II: more developed but still confined and may be palpable. Stage III: breaks through the capsule and may involve seminal vesicles. Stage IV: spreads to nearby organs or distant lymph nodes/bones.
Localized tumor: radical prostatectomy.
Radiotherapy may be an alternative, either external beam or brachytherapy.
Advanced cases: hormonal therapy/androgen deprivation.
Active surveillance: asymptomatic patients with life expectancy less than 10 years.
cases.trap: Stage III is extracapsular/seminal-vesicle spread; stage IV includes nearby organ or distant spread.
cases.memory: Confined I-II, capsule/seminal vesicles III, organs/nodes/bone IV.

cases.title: Androgen Deprivation Therapy
cases.scenario: A patient with advanced prostate cancer is planned for androgen deprivation therapy. Despite very low androgen levels, progression may eventually occur.
cases.ar: مريض advanced prostate cancer سيأخذ ADT، ومع الوقت قد يستمر نمو الورم رغم انخفاض androgen.
questions: State the surgical method of androgen deprivation.
List the medical methods in the lecture.
What eventual behavior of the tumor is mentioned?
For which prostate cancer group is hormonal therapy used?
answer: Surgical castration: bilateral orchidectomy.
Medical castration options listed: anti-androgens, LHRH agonists, the antagonist listed on the slide, and androgen receptor blockers.
Eventually the tumor may continue to grow even with undetectable androgen levels.
Hormonal therapy is used for advanced cases.
cases.trap: The slide contains the wording “LHRT antagonist”; the bank keeps the lecture concept without adding drugs not provided in the lecture.
cases.memory: Advanced cancer -> surgical or medical castration; progression may later occur despite low androgen.
